fields.title: From Clinical Question to Protocol
fields.description: Frame a clinically relevant question and turn it into an ethical, testable protocol.

fields.title: Design, Bias, and Study Readiness
fields.description: Select outcomes, protect study validity, and prepare a protocol for review.

fields.title: Writing an Answerable Clinical Question
fields.description: Use population, intervention, comparison, and outcome to make a research question precise.
fields.objectives:
Distinguish a clinical problem from a researchable question
Define a population and measurable outcome

content.value: A strong clinical question makes the population, exposure or intervention, comparison, and outcome visible. This lesson is educational and does not provide patient-specific medical advice.

fields.title: Choosing a Study Design
fields.description: Compare randomized, cohort, case-control, and pragmatic designs against the question and available evidence.
fields.objectives:
Compare common clinical study designs
Recognize feasibility and ethical constraints

content.value: Study design should follow the question, not the other way around. Compare the strength of inference, practical burden, and ethical safeguards before selecting a design.

fields.title: Endpoints, Recruitment, and Bias Control
fields.description: Define outcomes and recruitment safeguards that keep the protocol analysis-ready.
fields.objectives:
Separate primary and secondary endpoints
Plan recruitment and bias mitigation

content.value: Pre-specify endpoints, eligibility criteria, recruitment channels, and procedures for missing data. A transparent protocol helps reviewers understand what the study can and cannot conclude.

fields.title: Protocol Readiness Review
fields.description: Use a review checklist to identify gaps in governance, data quality, analysis, and participant protection.
fields.objectives:
Review a protocol for completeness
Prepare a concise study synopsis

content.value: Before submission, check the protocol against the research question, consent pathway, data management plan, statistical analysis plan, safety monitoring, and publication policy.

fields.title: Describing Clinical Data
fields.description: Build a sound descriptive foundation before choosing statistical tests.

fields.title: Uncertainty, Power, and Interpretation
fields.description: Interpret effect sizes, intervals, power, and regression without overstating evidence.

fields.title: Distributions and Descriptive Measures
fields.description: Choose summaries that reflect the shape and clinical meaning of a dataset.
fields.objectives:
Select appropriate descriptive measures
Describe distributions and missingness

content.value: Mean, median, spread, and graphical summaries answer different questions. Always inspect distribution, missingness, and measurement scale before reporting a number.

fields.title: Comparing Groups Responsibly
fields.description: Match common comparisons to the data structure and the research question.
fields.objectives:
Choose a comparison strategy
Report effect size and uncertainty

content.value: A statistical test does not replace clinical reasoning. Pair group comparisons with effect sizes, confidence intervals, assumptions, and a clear description of the population.

fields.title: Confidence Intervals and Statistical Power
fields.description: Connect uncertainty, sample size, and clinically meaningful effects.
fields.objectives:
Interpret confidence intervals
Explain power and sample-size trade-offs

content.value: Confidence intervals show the precision of an estimate; power planning addresses the ability to detect an effect under stated assumptions. Neither alone proves clinical importance.

fields.title: Regression and Transparent Reporting
fields.description: Use regression as a tool for estimation and communicate assumptions and limitations.
fields.objectives:
Identify confounding and model limitations
Write an evidence-aware statistical summary

content.value: Regression can adjust for measured covariates, but it cannot repair poor measurement, selection bias, or an unclear causal question. Report the model context and limitations.

fields.title: Question, Search, and Screening
fields.description: Create a focused review question and a reproducible search and screening process.

fields.title: Appraisal, Synthesis, and Certainty
fields.description: Assess risk of bias and communicate the certainty and limits of a synthesis.

fields.title: Building a Focused Review Question
fields.description: Use a structured question to define eligibility and prevent scope drift.
fields.objectives:
Define population, intervention, comparison, and outcome
Write inclusion and exclusion criteria

content.value: A focused review question sets the boundary for the search, screening, extraction, and synthesis. Document decisions before screening begins.

fields.title: Search Strategy and Screening Log
fields.description: Make discovery and screening reproducible with documented sources, dates, and decisions.
fields.objectives:
Document a reproducible search
Maintain a transparent screening log

content.value: Record databases, search dates, terms, deduplication, screening decisions, and reasons for exclusion. A clear audit trail makes the review easier to update and trust.

fields.title: Risk of Bias and Evidence Certainty
fields.description: Assess how design and execution affect confidence in each result.
fields.objectives:
Identify common sources of bias
Separate study quality from result size

content.value: Risk-of-bias judgments should be tied to the design and conduct of each study. Avoid reducing a nuanced appraisal to a single unqualified score.

fields.title: Evidence Tables and Responsible Synthesis
fields.description: Present study characteristics, findings, heterogeneity, and uncertainty clearly.
fields.objectives:
Build an evidence table
Communicate heterogeneity and limitations

content.value: A synthesis should show what was found, how consistent it was, and where uncertainty remains. Avoid claims that exceed the included evidence.

fields.title: Clinical Data and Problem Framing
fields.description: Understand clinical context, data provenance, and the question a model is meant to support.

fields.title: Validation, Bias, and Communication
fields.description: Evaluate models responsibly and communicate limitations to clinical stakeholders.

fields.title: Clinical Questions for AI Projects
fields.description: Define a useful clinical decision context before selecting a model or metric.
fields.objectives:
Describe the intended use and population
Identify safety and governance constraints

content.value: Responsible medical AI starts with a bounded clinical question, a defined population, and a clear account of who may be affected by an error.

fields.title: Data Provenance and Quality
fields.description: Trace source, labeling, missingness, shift, and representativeness in clinical data.
fields.objectives:
Describe data provenance
Detect quality and representativeness risks

content.value: Clinical data reflects care pathways, documentation habits, and access patterns. Record provenance and check whether the development data represents the intended use population.

fields.title: Model Validation and Bias
fields.description: Compare validation strategies and examine subgroup performance without hiding uncertainty.
fields.objectives:
Distinguish internal and external validation
Assess subgroup performance and bias

content.value: Validation is a design problem as much as a metric problem. Examine temporal, geographic, and subgroup performance, and state uncertainty around every estimate.

fields.title: Explainability and Safe Communication
fields.description: Communicate model behavior and limitations without presenting research output as clinical advice.
fields.objectives:
Explain model limitations to stakeholders
Separate research evaluation from clinical deployment

content.value: Explanations should clarify what a model used and what it cannot establish. Educational examples are not a substitute for clinical validation, governance, or professional judgment.

fields.title: Manuscript Structure and Story
fields.description: Build a coherent scientific narrative from question, methods, results, and interpretation.

fields.title: Tables, Figures, and Responsible Assistance
fields.description: Improve clarity while preserving authorship, evidence, and publication integrity.

fields.title: IMRaD as a Research Narrative
fields.description: Align introduction, methods, results, and discussion with the research question.
fields.objectives:
Plan an IMRaD structure
Keep claims aligned with methods and results

content.value: A manuscript is an argument supported by evidence. Each section should answer its role in the narrative while avoiding claims that the design cannot support.

fields.title: Abstracts and Results That Stay Precise
fields.description: Write concise abstracts and results that distinguish estimates, uncertainty, and interpretation.
fields.objectives:
Draft a structured abstract
Report results without overstating significance

content.value: Readers should be able to identify the question, design, population, main result, and uncertainty quickly. Keep interpretation in the discussion rather than embedding it in the result.

fields.title: Tables and Figures as Evidence
fields.description: Choose visual forms that make evidence easier to inspect and reproduce.
fields.objectives:
Match a visual to the question
Write complete captions and notes

content.value: A good table or figure reduces cognitive load without hiding uncertainty. Label denominators, units, missing values, and analysis populations clearly.

fields.title: Responsible AI Assistance and Authorship
fields.description: Use writing assistance transparently without delegating evidence judgment or authorship responsibility.
fields.objectives:
Identify acceptable assistance workflows
Protect confidentiality and authorship integrity

content.value: AI assistance must not replace source verification, clinical reasoning, or author accountability. Follow the target journal and institution policy, and do not upload confidential manuscripts or identifiable data.

fields.title: Ethics, Consent, and Good Clinical Practice
fields.description: Ground study work in participant protection, governance, and responsible conduct.

fields.title: Data Stewardship and Publication Integrity
fields.description: Protect records and make authorship, reporting, peer review, and corrections trustworthy.

fields.title: Consent and Participant Protection
fields.description: Connect informed consent, risk minimization, privacy, and respectful participation.
fields.objectives:
Describe essential consent elements
Recognize participant-protection responsibilities

content.value: Consent is an ongoing process, not only a signature. Research teams should explain purpose, procedures, risks, benefits, alternatives, privacy, and voluntary participation in accessible language.

fields.title: Good Clinical Practice in Daily Work
fields.description: Translate GCP principles into documentation, delegation, safety, and quality practices.
fields.objectives:
Identify essential study records
Connect responsibilities to quality management

content.value: Good Clinical Practice supports participant rights, reliable data, and accountable study conduct. Apply local regulations, approved protocols, and institutional procedures.

fields.title: Data Stewardship and Reproducibility
fields.description: Plan secure, traceable, and reproducible handling of research data and records.
fields.objectives:
Describe a data-management lifecycle
Protect confidentiality and traceability

content.value: Good stewardship covers collection, access, quality checks, versioning, retention, sharing, and destruction. Use approved systems and minimize identifiable data.

fields.title: Authorship, Peer Review, and Corrections
fields.description: Handle contribution, review, reporting, and correction decisions with integrity.
fields.objectives:
Distinguish authorship from acknowledgment
Respond transparently to errors and concerns

content.value: Agree contributions early, disclose conflicts, preserve reviewer confidentiality, and correct the record when errors are found. Follow journal and institutional policies.
